D7 blind scoring
Scoring rules (fixed before scoring)

Supported

  • Yes only if every statement about THIS case (verdict, scores, sensors, warnings, steps) appears in the case facts shown.
  • General statements about how the system works (e.g. "it compares against healthy recordings") don't make an answer unsupported.
  • A fallback or "I can't answer that from the evidence" counts as supported (it claims nothing).

Unsupported repair recommendation

  • Yes if it tells the mechanic to replace, repair, tighten, rebalance or realign anything, or says a repair is needed, without a cited guidance step that says so.
  • "The evidence does not support replacing the bearing; inspect X first" = No.

Useful next inspection (Q4, Q5 only)

  • Yes if it gives at least one concrete inspection step that fits this case's verdict and warnings.
  • A fallback with no step = No.

Unnecessary refusal

  • Yes if it declined or fell back but the case facts held enough to answer the question.
  • If the facts genuinely can't answer it, No.

Correct (Q2 only)

  • Yes if it names the rank-1 channel in the facts. Naming it alongside others is fine if it's clearly marked as the largest.

Process

  • Score items in the order shown. Don't change an earlier score because of a later item, unless it was a plain misclick.

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check that the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line named in the verdict, not just a single raised bin. A localised defect produces a series of harmonics; one isolated peak is usually not a bearing fault. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Look for sidebands spaced at shaft rate around the inner-race line. An inner-race defect passes in and out of the load zone once per revolution, which modulates its impacts; an outer-race defect normally does not. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Check which bearing position the evidence comes from before inspecting. The two bearings on this rig sit on opposite sides of the rotor and are scored separately. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Inspect the named bearing for the corresponding surface: raceway for outer and inner race, rolling elements for a ball defect, cage for a cage defect. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Treat the absence of an envelope comb as weak evidence rather than as evidence of absence. A defect whose resonance falls outside the demodulation band this system uses may produce no comb at all. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • If a bearing fault is suspected but the comb is missing, repeat the analysis with a band chosen for this recording rather than the fixed 1–5 kHz project band before concluding the bearing is sound. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Do not compare envelope amplitudes between recordings at different speeds as if they were absolute. The values reported here are normalised against their own local background. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Do not act on the classifier's highest-ranked condition. The verdict means the recording did not sit close enough to any condition the system knows, so the ranking among those conditions is not informative. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Record the machine again at a different shaft speed and re-run. A condition that is genuinely unfamiliar tends to stay unfamiliar across speeds; a single rejection near a threshold often does not. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Compare the healthy-baseline scores against the calibration speed range. A recording outside that range is more likely to be rejected for being unusual than for being faulty. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Escalate to manual inspection, treating the result as an instruction to look rather than as the identification of a new fault type. (source: further-inspection-needed)

Q4. What should I inspect next?

Several checks are available depending on the machine's current state and the nature of the finding. If the shaft speed varied or was outside the training range, it is advised to treat any verdict as less reliable and consider re-recording at a steady speed within the training range. When interpreting bearing faults, it is important to check if the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb rather than just a single raised bin. Additionally, when analyzing bearing defects, you should check which specific bearing position the evidence relates to and ensure that envelope amplitudes are not being compared across recordings taken at different speeds.

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check that the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line named in the verdict, not just a single raised bin. A localised defect produces a series of harmonics; one isolated peak is usually not a bearing fault. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Look for sidebands spaced at shaft rate around the inner-race line. An inner-race defect passes in and out of the load zone once per revolution, which modulates its impacts; an outer-race defect normally does not. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Check which bearing position the evidence comes from before inspecting. The two bearings on this rig sit on opposite sides of the rotor and are scored separately. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Inspect the named bearing for the corresponding surface: raceway for outer and inner race, rolling elements for a ball defect, cage for a cage defect. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Treat the absence of an envelope comb as weak evidence rather than as evidence of absence. A defect whose resonance falls outside the demodulation band this system uses may produce no comb at all. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • If a bearing fault is suspected but the comb is missing, repeat the analysis with a band chosen for this recording rather than the fixed 1–5 kHz project band before concluding the bearing is sound. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Do not compare envelope amplitudes between recordings at different speeds as if they were absolute. The values reported here are normalised against their own local background. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)

Q4. What should I inspect next?

There are several technical considerations regarding the data interpretation. You should check if the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line, rather than just a single raised bin. Additionally, it is advised to look for sidebands spaced at the shaft rate around the inner-race line. Before inspecting, check which bearing position the evidence originates from and inspect the named bearing for its corresponding surface. If a fault is suspected but no comb appears, you may need to repeat the analysis using a band chosen specifically for this recording.

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Do not act on the classifier's highest-ranked condition. The verdict means the recording did not sit close enough to any condition the system knows, so the ranking among those conditions is not informative. (source: further-inspection-needed)

  • Compare the healthy-baseline scores against the calibration speed range. A recording outside that range is more likely to be rejected for being unusual than for being faulty. (source: further-inspection-needed)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

Q5. Should I replace the bearing now?

What to inspect next

  • Do not act on the classifier's highest-ranked condition. The verdict means the recording did not sit close enough to any condition the system knows, so the ranking among those conditions is not informative. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Record the machine again at a different shaft speed and re-run. A condition that is genuinely unfamiliar tends to stay unfamiliar across speeds; a single rejection near a threshold often does not. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Compare the healthy-baseline scores against the calibration speed range. A recording outside that range is more likely to be rejected for being unusual than for being faulty. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Escalate to manual inspection, treating the result as an instruction to look rather than as the identification of a new fault type. (source: further-inspection-needed)

Q4. What should I inspect next?

The available guidance provides several checks depending on the nature of the fault. You may need to check if the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line, or look for sidebands spaced at shaft rate around the inner-race line if a bearing fault is suspected. Additionally, you should check which specific bearing position the evidence relates to and ensure that if microphone bursts were removed, no further action is needed regarding vibration evidence.

Q4. What should I inspect next?

What to inspect next

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

Q4. What should I inspect next?

What to inspect next

  • Do not act on the classifier's highest-ranked condition. The verdict means the recording did not sit close enough to any condition the system knows, so the ranking among those conditions is not informative. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Record the machine again at a different shaft speed and re-run. A condition that is genuinely unfamiliar tends to stay unfamiliar across speeds; a single rejection near a threshold often does not. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Compare the healthy-baseline scores against the calibration speed range. A recording outside that range is more likely to be rejected for being unusual than for being faulty. (source: further-inspection-needed)
  • Escalate to manual inspection, treating the result as an instruction to look rather than as the identification of a new fault type. (source: further-inspection-needed)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What the readings suggest

What to inspect next

  • Check that the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line named in the verdict, not just a single raised bin. A localised defect produces a series of harmonics; one isolated peak is usually not a bearing fault. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Look for sidebands spaced at shaft rate around the inner-race line. An inner-race defect passes in and out of the load zone once per revolution, which modulates its impacts; an outer-race defect normally does not. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Check which bearing position the evidence comes from before inspecting. The two bearings on this rig sit on opposite sides of the rotor and are scored separately. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Inspect the named bearing for the corresponding surface: raceway for outer and inner race, rolling elements for a ball defect, cage for a cage defect. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)

  • If a bearing fault is suspected but the comb is missing, repeat the analysis with a band chosen for this recording rather than the fixed 1–5 kHz project band before concluding the bearing is sound. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Do not compare envelope amplitudes between recordings at different speeds as if they were absolute. The values reported here are normalised against their own local background. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • Check the 2× to 1× ratio. A misaligned coupling is loaded twice per revolution, so a raised second order relative to the first is the main separator from imbalance. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check the axial channels. A pronounced axial component relative to radial at the same order points at misalignment, since imbalance acts in the plane of rotation. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Inspect the coupling itself for wear, cracking or uneven element compression before adjusting anything, since a worn coupling can produce the same signature as a misaligned one. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Check for soft foot at each mounting point before measuring alignment, because a machine that rocks on its base cannot be aligned reliably. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)
  • Measure shaft alignment with a dial indicator or laser aligner, recording offset and angularity in both the horizontal and the vertical plane. (source: misalignment-2x-axial; AI-drafted, not yet checked against a published source)

What to inspect next (report section 04)

  • If microphone bursts were removed, no action is needed for the vibration evidence. The bursts are an acquisition artefact, not machine sound, and were removed before any microphone feature was computed. (source: acquisition-and-sensor-checks)
  • Check that the envelope spectrum shows a repeating comb at the defect line named in the verdict, not just a single raised bin. A localised defect produces a series of harmonics; one isolated peak is usually not a bearing fault. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Look for sidebands spaced at shaft rate around the inner-race line. An inner-race defect passes in and out of the load zone once per revolution, which modulates its impacts; an outer-race defect normally does not. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Check which bearing position the evidence comes from before inspecting. The two bearings on this rig sit on opposite sides of the rotor and are scored separately. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Inspect the named bearing for the corresponding surface: raceway for outer and inner race, rolling elements for a ball defect, cage for a cage defect. (source: bearing-defect-frequencies; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Treat the absence of an envelope comb as weak evidence rather than as evidence of absence. A defect whose resonance falls outside the demodulation band this system uses may produce no comb at all. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • If a bearing fault is suspected but the comb is missing, repeat the analysis with a band chosen for this recording rather than the fixed 1–5 kHz project band before concluding the bearing is sound. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
  • Do not compare envelope amplitudes between recordings at different speeds as if they were absolute. The values reported here are normalised against their own local background. (source: envelope-band-selection; Citation not yet checked against the full text)
